items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the breakdown of rock by repeated expansion and contraction caused by large daily temperature changes”.
items.answer: Insolation weathering (thermal fracture)
items.markingKey: Insolation weathering (thermal fracture): the breakdown of rock by repeated expansion and contraction caused by large daily temperature changes. [1]

items.stem: Explain the process of salt weathering.
items.answer: Saline water enters pores and cracks; evaporation causes crystals to grow, exerting pressure; heating makes salts expand and hydration makes them swell; repeated cycles break off grains and flakes.

items.stem: Explain why the importance of insolation weathering has been questioned.
items.answer: Experiments show heating and cooling of dry rock causes little breakdown; water (dew, rain) is usually needed, so chemical and salt processes may be more important; but very large and rapid changes can cause stress.

items.stem: In an experiment, four blocks of limestone were soaked in different solutions, dried at 60 °C, and the cycle repeated 20 times. Initial and final masses (g): distilled water: 100.4 to 99.8; sodium chloride solution: 102.7 to 100.1; sodium sulphate solution: 103.2 to 89; magnesium sulphate solution: 97.2 to 87.8. Explain why the block in distilled water lost very little mass.
items.answer: No salt crystals grow in the pores, so there is no crystallisation pressure; only slight wetting and drying.

items.stem: In an experiment, four blocks of granite were soaked in different solutions, dried at 60 °C, and the cycle repeated 30 times. Initial and final masses (g): distilled water: 101.3 to 101; sodium chloride solution: 104.3 to 99.9; sodium sulphate solution: 103.7 to 92.2; magnesium sulphate solution: 98.6 to 92.5. (a) Explain why the block in distilled water lost very little mass. (b) Suggest how the experiment could be made more reliable.
items.answer: (a) No salt crystals grow in the pores, so there is no crystallisation pressure; only slight wetting and drying. (b) Repeat with several blocks per solution; use blocks of the same size and porosity; control temperature and drying time; weigh accurately after each cycle.

items.stem: Elena argues that weathering in hot deserts is mainly the result of high temperatures. How far do you agree? Support your answer with examples. In your answer you may refer to experiments, rock type and salt weathering.
items.answer: For: Large diurnal temperature ranges cause thermal stress, exfoliation and granular disintegration. Against: Experiments show heat alone is ineffective; moisture is essential for salt crystallisation, hydration and chemical processes; rock type and structure influence rates. Conclusion: Temperature changes contribute, but moisture, especially salt solutions, is the critical factor in most desert weathering.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the peeling away of curved sheets from a rock surface, often linked to thermal stress and the release of pressure”.
items.answer: Exfoliation
items.markingKey: Exfoliation: the peeling away of curved sheets from a rock surface, often linked to thermal stress and the release of pressure. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “Water plays a role in most desert weathering.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. Dew, fog and occasional rain enable salt, chemical and thermal processes.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain why weathering rates are generally slow in hot deserts.
items.answer: Lack of water limits chemical weathering; little vegetation and organic acids; but where moisture is present (dew, salt), weathering can be locally rapid.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the removal of loose, fine material by wind, which can lower the land surface and form hollows”.
items.answer: Deflation
items.markingKey: Deflation: the removal of loose, fine material by wind, which can lower the land surface and form hollows. [1]

items.stem: Explain how wind transports sand.
items.answer: Above a threshold velocity, grains are lifted; most move by saltation in short hops; impacts push larger grains along the surface (surface creep/reptation); fine dust travels in suspension.

items.stem: Explain the formation of a barchan dune.
items.answer: Wind blows sand up the gentle windward slope; at the crest it falls down the steep slip face (about 32-34°); the edges move faster as they contain less sand, forming horns pointing downwind; forms where sand supply is limited.

items.stem: Assess the view that wind is the most important agent in the formation of desert landforms.
items.answer: For: Wind forms dunes and ergs, deflation hollows (Qattara Depression), yardangs, zeugen and ventifacts. Against: Water, from rare floods and from wetter past climates, forms wadis, alluvial fans, pediments, playas and mesas and buttes; weathering prepares material. Conclusion: Wind is locally dominant, but water, past and present, is more important in shaping most desert landscapes.

items.stem: Explain the formation of zeugen and yardangs.
items.answer: Abrasion by wind-blown sand attacks rock near the ground; zeugen form where horizontal resistant strata cap softer rock, undercut along joints; yardangs form in vertical bands parallel to the wind, streamlined by abrasion and deflation.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a steep-sided, flat-floored valley in a desert, dry for most of the year but carrying flash floods after storms”.
items.answer: Wadi
items.markingKey: Wadi: a steep-sided, flat-floored valley in a desert, dry for most of the year but carrying flash floods after storms. [1]

items.stem: Explain the formation of an alluvial fan.
items.answer: A stream emerges from a confined mountain canyon onto a plain; the channel widens and gradient falls; velocity drops and infiltration reduces discharge, so sediment is deposited, coarse near the apex and fine further out; channels shift, building a cone.

items.stem: Explain why wadis have steep sides and flat floors.
items.answer: Flash floods carry a large load and erode vertically and laterally; banks have little vegetation and collapse; sediment is spread across the floor as floods wane.

items.stem: Fig. 14.3 shows discharge (m³/s) in a wadi near Jeddah, Saudi Arabia after a thunderstorm whose peak rainfall occurred at 1.5 hours: 0 h: 0, 1 h: 8, 2 h: 31, 3 h: 102, 4 h: 49, 5 h: 19, 6 h: 5, 8 h: 2, 10 h: 0. Before the storm the channel was dry. Suggest why flash floods are a hazard in desert towns.
items.answer: Little warning; people and roads in dry wadi beds; high sediment loads damage property; drivers underestimate depth (e.g. Jeddah 2009).

items.answer: (a) 93 m³/s per hour (b) Little warning; people and roads in dry wadi beds; high sediment loads damage property; drivers underestimate depth (e.g. Jeddah 2009).

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that present-day processes can explain most desert landforms?
items.answer: For: Flash floods form wadis, alluvial fans and playas today; wind shapes dunes; weathering continues. Against: Many features (large wadis, pediments, inselbergs, fossil dunes, lake shorelines) formed under wetter or different climates; present rates are too slow to explain them. Conclusion: Present processes modify desert landscapes, but many major landforms are inherited from past climates.

items.stem: Explain the formation of a playa.
items.answer: Streams flow into an enclosed basin after storms; a temporary lake forms; evaporation leaves fine sediment and salts; the flat surface is re-flooded only occasionally.

items.stem: Fig. 14.3 shows discharge (m³/s) in a wadi near Jeddah, Saudi Arabia after a thunderstorm whose peak rainfall occurred at 0.5 hours: 0 h: 0, 1 h: 47, 2 h: 281, 3 h: 141, 4 h: 79, 5 h: 33, 6 h: 17, 8 h: 10, 10 h: 3. Table 4.1 gives, for each dune, the dune height (m) and the migration distance (m per year). Dune 1: 3.5, 60. Dune 2: 10.2, 40. Dune 3: 12.4, 45. Dune 4: 13.8, 41. Dune 5: 15.2, 38. Dune 6: 16.9, 35. Dune 7: 24.6, 14. Dune 8: 26.4, 8. Critical values of rs for n = 8: 0.643 (0.05 level) and 0.833 (0.01 level). Suggest one limitation of the method and how the investigation could be improved.
items.answer: Wind speed and sand supply may differ between dunes; measure over several years and choose dunes in one dune field.

items.stem: A study recorded the height above the ground and the depth of abrasion grooves on a yardang at 11 points. Table 4.1 gives, for each point, the height above ground (cm) and the groove depth (mm). Point 1: 21, 35. Point 2: 30, 39. Point 3: 32, 27. Point 4: 45, 40. Point 5: 150, 22. Point 6: 152, 6. Point 7: 167, 19. Point 8: 178, 24. Point 9: 196, 1. Point 10: 205, 4. Point 11: 249, 18. Critical values of rs for n = 11: 0.536 (0.05 level) and 0.709 (0.01 level). (a) State a suitable null hypothesis for this investigation. (b) Suggest reasons for the relationship shown by the data.
items.answer: (a) There is no relationship between the height above ground (cm) and the groove depth (mm). (b) Most sand moves by saltation close to the ground, so abrasion is greatest near the base and declines with height.

items.stem: With the help of examples, evaluate the claim that wind is the most important agent in the formation of desert landforms. In your answer you may refer to wadis and weathering.
items.answer: For: Wind forms dunes and ergs, deflation hollows (Qattara Depression), yardangs, zeugen and ventifacts. Against: Water, from rare floods and from wetter past climates, forms wadis, alluvial fans, pediments, playas and mesas and buttes; weathering prepares material. Conclusion: Wind is locally dominant, but water, past and present, is more important in shaping most desert landscapes.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “wadi”?
options: A steep-sided, flat-floored valley in a desert, dry for most of the year but carrying flash floods after storms.
A sudden, short-lived flood following an intense storm, with a very steep rising limb.
A cone of sediment deposited where a mountain stream emerges onto a plain and loses energy.
A continuous slope formed by alluvial fans joining together along a mountain front.
items.answer: A steep-sided, flat-floored valley in a desert, dry for most of the year but carrying flash floods after storms.
items.markingKey: Wadi: a steep-sided, flat-floored valley in a desert, dry for most of the year but carrying flash floods after storms. [1]

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “Flash floods have long lag times.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Lag times are very short because overland flow is rapid.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain the formation of an alluvial fan. (b) A revision website states: “Pediments are formed only by wind.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) A stream emerges from a confined mountain canyon onto a plain; the channel widens and gradient falls; velocity drops and infiltration reduces discharge, so sediment is deposited, coarse near the apex and fine further out; channels shift, building a cone. (b) Not correct. They are thought to result mainly from sheet floods, weathering and scarp retreat.

items.stem: With the help of examples, evaluate the claim that present-day processes can explain most desert landforms. In your answer you may refer to pluvial periods, wind and equifinality.
items.answer: For: Flash floods form wadis, alluvial fans and playas today; wind shapes dunes; weathering continues. Against: Many features (large wadis, pediments, inselbergs, fossil dunes, lake shorelines) formed under wetter or different climates; present rates are too slow to explain them. Conclusion: Present processes modify desert landscapes, but many major landforms are inherited from past climates.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the growth of salt crystals in rock pores as water evaporates, exerting pressure that breaks the rock”.
items.answer: Salt crystallisation

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain the process of salt weathering. (b) Explain why the importance of insolation weathering has been questioned.
items.answer: (a) Saline water enters pores and cracks; evaporation causes crystals to grow, exerting pressure; heating makes salts expand and hydration makes them swell; repeated cycles break off grains and flakes. (b) Experiments show heating and cooling of dry rock causes little breakdown; water (dew, rain) is usually needed, so chemical and salt processes may be more important; but very large and rapid changes can cause stress.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain the process of salt weathering. (b) A student writes: “Water plays a role in most desert weathering.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Saline water enters pores and cracks; evaporation causes crystals to grow, exerting pressure; heating makes salts expand and hydration makes them swell; repeated cycles break off grains and flakes. (b) Correct. Dew, fog and occasional rain enable salt, chemical and thermal processes.

items.stem: In an experiment, four blocks of limestone were soaked in different solutions, dried at 60 °C, and the cycle repeated 20 times. Initial and final masses (g): distilled water: 95.3 to 95.2; sodium chloride solution: 96.4 to 91.1; sodium sulphate solution: 98.8 to 86.5; magnesium sulphate solution: 96.3 to 83.7. Explain why the block in distilled water lost very little mass.
items.answer: No salt crystals grow in the pores, so there is no crystallisation pressure; only slight wetting and drying.

items.stem: In an experiment, four blocks of granite were soaked in different solutions, dried at 60 °C, and the cycle repeated 20 times. Initial and final masses (g): distilled water: 107.4 to 106.9; sodium chloride solution: 105.9 to 101.5; sodium sulphate solution: 107 to 76.8; magnesium sulphate solution: 106.1 to 91. (a) Identify the most effective solution and calculate the mean loss per cycle in grams. (b) Explain why the block in distilled water lost very little mass.
items.answer: (a) sodium sulphate solution: 1.51 g per cycle (b) No salt crystals grow in the pores, so there is no crystallisation pressure; only slight wetting and drying.

items.stem: Chloe argues that weathering in hot deserts is mainly the result of high temperatures. How far do you agree? Support your answer with examples. In your answer you may refer to rock type, salt weathering and experiments.
items.answer: For: Large diurnal temperature ranges cause thermal stress, exfoliation and granular disintegration. Against: Experiments show heat alone is ineffective; moisture is essential for salt crystallisation, hydration and chemical processes; rock type and structure influence rates. Conclusion: Temperature changes contribute, but moisture, especially salt solutions, is the critical factor in most desert weathering.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) A revision website states: “Ergs (sand seas) cover most of the Sahara.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain the formation of zeugen and yardangs.
items.answer: (a) Not correct. They cover about a fifth; most is rocky or stony desert. (b) Abrasion by wind-blown sand attacks rock near the ground; zeugen form where horizontal resistant strata cap softer rock, undercut along joints; yardangs form in vertical bands parallel to the wind, streamlined by abrasion and deflation.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain the formation of a playa. (b) Explain the formation of an alluvial fan.
items.answer: (a) Streams flow into an enclosed basin after storms; a temporary lake forms; evaporation leaves fine sediment and salts; the flat surface is re-flooded only occasionally.
